p.x:
My name is Ben. I work from home three days a week. My office is the spare room, but sometimes I work at the kitchen table because it's sunny there.
Every morning, I log in at eight o'clock and check my calendar. I usually have a video call with my team at nine. I wear headphones so I can hear everyone clearly. Sometimes the wifi is slow and the connection breaks!
At five o'clock, I log off. My friends joke that I work in my pyjamas, but it isn't true. I always get dressed. Sitting all day can give me backache, so I go for a walk at lunchtime.

Since 2020, millions of people have started working outside the office. Many companies now let staff work from home for part of the week. Meetings happen on video calls, where people mute their microphone when they aren't speaking and turn on their webcam so colleagues can see them. When someone needs to show a document, they share their screen.
There are many perks. People save time and money on travel, and some move to cheaper areas. Freelancers can work for clients all over the world, although working across time zones means some meetings happen late at night. Files are stored in the cloud, so everyone can access them from anywhere.
However, remote work has its problems. Technical issues are common: if your computer freezes, you might have to reboot it in the middle of a meeting. Many people complain that their inbox is always full and that it's hard to switch off when your home is also your office. Long hours in front of a screen can cause eye strain, and some workers feel isolation because they rarely see colleagues.
To stay organised, teams often show their status online, such as "available" or "in a meeting", and ask each other about their availability before planning work. Experts advise workers to take regular breaks and create a clear end to the working day.

The rise of remote work has transformed not only where people work but how they think about work itself. In cities like Chiang Mai and Bali, communities of digital nomads travel the world while earning money online, often renting a desk in a coworking space where they can meet other professionals. For many of them, freedom and flexibility matter more than a stable career in one place.
Yet working remotely demands considerable self-discipline. Without a manager nearby, workers must organise their own time and resist the distractions of home. Many teams have adopted asynchronous communication, in which colleagues leave messages and respond when they can rather than meeting in real time. This suits people in different countries but can slow down decisions. Even small technical problems, such as limited bandwidth or lag on a video call, can make collaboration frustrating.
Health is another concern. Few home offices are designed for long hours of work, and doctors report rising numbers of back and neck problems among people who work on sofas or at kitchen tables. An ergonomic chair and a properly positioned screen can make a significant difference.
For employers, remote work raises questions of trust and security. Some companies monitor their employees' computers, a practice many workers find intrusive. Cybersecurity is a serious issue, too, which is why staff are often required to use a VPN. Meanwhile, the growth of the gig economy means that more people now work as independent contractors, sending an invoice for each job rather than receiving a regular salary, and often without sick pay or holiday benefits.
